name: Dawson v. Delaware
question: Whether Delaware violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments by introducing the stipulated Aryan Brotherhood membership evidence at capital sentencing; no challenge to the convictions is decided.
facts: Dawson and the murder victim were white. The parties stipulated that the Aryan Brotherhood began as a racist California prison gang and that a separate gang with that name existed in Delaware. The stipulation and tattoo evidence did not establish the Delaware organization’s violent conduct or aims, an organizational connection with the crime, or racial motivation for this murder. Dawson preserved his constitutional objection to the agreed evidentiary presentation. His mitigation included family kindness and participation in drug and alcohol programs; the State established three statutory aggravators. Delaware upheld the death sentence, treating the membership evidence as relevant to character and mitigation. Dawson seeks relief from that sentence; Delaware defends relevance and alternatively raises harmless error. The stipulation is not evidence of every fact about other prison gangs.
entering: First and Fourteenth Amendment protection of association; NAACP v. Alabama, 357 U.S. 449, and Bates v. Little Rock, 361 U.S. 516. Abel, 469 U.S. 45, permits association evidence tied to witness bias; Barclay, 463 U.S. 939, permits consideration of demonstrated racial motivation for the crime. Zant, 462 U.S. 862, distinguishes legitimate sentencing considerations from constitutionally protected beliefs used as aggravation in themselves. Payne, 501 U.S. 808, permits responsive mitigation rebuttal; it does not dispense with relevance. Chapman, 386 U.S. 18, supplies the beyond-reasonable-doubt standard where constitutional harmless-error review is available; availability for this particular error remains an issue. The simulated Simon & Schuster decision of December 10 preserves neutral remedies while rejecting its identified speech-based restraint, and does not create an evidentiary exclusion. Estelle of December 4 distinguishes state evidentiary error from constitutional deprivation. Neither displaces the association/relevance inquiry.
action: The judgment sustaining the death sentence is vacated and the case remanded, 8–1. The convictions remain intact.

votes.remedy: Delaware must conduct further proceedings consistent with the constitutional relevance ruling; convictions remain intact.

Stone would require Chapman review and a new sentencing proceeding unless the State proves harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt. Thomas would affirm the sentence without reaching a remedial inquiry.

opinions.name: Opinion of the Court, Part A
opinions.author: White
opinions.scope: Constitutional relevance and application; supports sentence-only vacatur.

opinions.name: Opinion of the Court, Part B
opinions.author: White
opinions.scope: Remand leaving both the availability and application of harmless-error review open.

opinions.name: Concurrence in part and in the judgment
opinions.author: Stone
opinions.scope: Joins Part A and the vacatur; would require trial-record Chapman review and new sentencing unless Delaware satisfies its burden.

opinions.name: Concurrence
opinions.author: Blackmun
opinions.scope: Joins both Court parts; emphasizes that whether harmless-error treatment is permissible for this error remains open.

opinions.name: Dissent
opinions.author: Thomas
opinions.scope: Would affirm because prison-gang membership permits an adverse character inference and can rebut mitigation.

holdings.title: Protected association must bear on a legitimate sentencing issue
holdings.rule: The State may not use protected association to aggravate a capital sentence when the evidence establishes only abstract beliefs and supplies no supported connection to the crime, future danger, another legitimate sentencing issue, or the mitigation actually offered. The stipulated association evidence here lacks that connection and its admission violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments.
holdings.part: Part A of White’s opinion; Stone, Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter join White at this level of generality.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that an unpopular association does not become sentencing evidence merely because its beliefs are objectionable. NAACP and Bates protect association; Abel shows that those protections do not exclude evidence that actually establishes a witness’s bias. Barclay likewise involved demonstrated racial motivation for the crime. This stipulation supplies neither connection. Even assuming that the Delaware group shared racist beliefs, the State established no link between those beliefs and this murder, and no violent organizational objective attributable to Dawson. The evidence also does not contradict his actual mitigation concerning family kindness and participation in rehabilitation programs. Payne permits relevant rebuttal, not punishment for a belief labeled bad character. Zant’s distinction between legitimate aggravation and protected beliefs therefore controls the application. The Court announces no universal bar against evidence of association and no rule that a white victim always excludes racial motive. A materially different evidentiary record may establish relevance that this stipulation does not.
precedents: NAACP v. Alabama, 357 U.S. 449 — applied: freedom of association protects unpopular affiliations.
Bates v. Little Rock, 361 U.S. 516 — applied: protected association cannot itself justify adverse governmental treatment.
United States v. Abel, 469 U.S. 45 — distinguished on the facts: association established witness bias there; relevant association remains admissible.
Barclay v. Florida, 463 U.S. 939 — distinguished: demonstrated racial motivation connected the association to the crime.
Zant v. Stephens, 462 U.S. 862 — applied: protected beliefs cannot themselves supply an aggravating circumstance.
Payne v. Tennessee, 501 U.S. 808 — applied with its relevance limit: rebuttal of mitigation does not make unrelated belief probative.
Schware v. Board of Bar Examiners, 353 U.S. 232 — applied by analogy: an affiliation without a rational connection to the relevant character inquiry is insufficient.

holdings.title: Scope of the remand
holdings.rule: The state judgment sustaining this sentence cannot stand on the constitutional reasoning it adopted. On remand the state court may consider Delaware’s harmless-error contention; this Court decides neither whether harmless-error analysis is available for this violation nor whether the error was harmless.
holdings.part: Part B of White’s opinion, joined by Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter; seven Justices control the remand’s reserved scope.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that correction of the constitutional error requires vacating the judgment that sustained the sentence, while leaving the convictions intact. The relevance ruling answers the question reviewed here. It does not establish how the challenged evidence affected this jury’s sentencing decision, and it does not decide every condition under which constitutional evidentiary error can be harmless. Delaware advanced harmlessness as an alternative ground, but the state court did not decide that contention under the constitutional rule now stated. Chapman supplies a demanding burden when its form of harmless-error review applies; citing that framework does not decide its availability for this particular infringement. The proper course is to permit consideration of the issue on remand without prejudging either branch. Neither the existence of other aggravators nor the Court’s finding of irrelevance supplies an automatic harmlessness finding. Conversely, the Court does not now command a new sentencing hearing regardless of further lawful review.
precedents: Chapman v. California, 386 U.S. 18 — preserved: its constitutional harmless-error burden is not relaxed; applicability and satisfaction in this case remain undecided.

after: Effective March 9, the constitutional relevance rule is applied to this stipulation; no categorical association-evidence ban is added. The remand’s seven-Justice reservation leaves both availability and application of harmless-error treatment open. Stone’s mandatory Chapman/new-sentencing sequence is not the Court’s instruction. No earlier simulated rule is displaced.
separate: Stone concurs in the relevance ruling and vacatur but would require Delaware to prove harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt on the trial record, with new sentencing otherwise. Blackmun joins the Court and emphasizes that the permissibility of harmless-error treatment itself remains unresolved; this safeguard may protect against chilling association as well as an unreliable sentence. Thomas dissents: voluntary prison-gang membership can support a character and future-danger inference and rebut favorable character evidence. He would treat ordinary evidentiary fairness, rather than a categorical First Amendment insulation, as the inquiry. His inference is not a Court finding about this Delaware group.
procedure: Supreme Court review of the sentence ends; the case returns to Delaware for further proceedings. No resentencing date, harmlessness finding, stay, or retained Supreme Court supervision is created. The convictions remain intact.
stoneCheck: The approved core fixes sentence-only vacatur and trial-record Chapman review with new sentencing unless Delaware meets its burden. Part A matches that core; Part B leaves more open than Stone permits. Stone therefore joins Part A and the vacating judgment but states his distinct remand instruction separately. His position is neither broadened into categorical exclusion nor narrowed to the Court’s remedy reservation. The historical comparator’s open harmlessness question is not a changed trial premise requiring a new Stone choice: it is the other Justices’ competing remedy position.
assignment: Stone is in the sentence-vacatur coalition and assigns White. White’s separate remand discussion retains seven votes. No circulation change to a non-Stone commitment is needed.
audit: White; Stevens; O’Connor; Scalia; Kennedy; Souter
Vacate/remand on the relevance boundary in Abel, Barclay and Zant.
Same disposition and controlling relevance ground after comparator; all retain the open remand question.
Blackmun
Vacate/remand; constitutional association/relevance ground, with special remedial concern.
Joins Court; official concurrence supports reserving whether harmless-error treatment is possible. Provisional suggestion of a new-sentencing preference is not treated as a fixed demand.
Thomas
Affirm; relevant inference from voluntary gang affiliation, rebuttal and character.
Retained after official dissent review; no factual finding about unproved gang violence is manufactured.
alternatives: Relevance-based exclusion and affirmance based on gang-character inference are the competing paths. The majority refuses to substitute an inference about another organization for this stipulation’s content; Thomas regards the voluntary prison-gang identity itself as probative. Automatic new sentencing and an immediate harmlessness finding both exceed the seven-Justice remedial agreement. Stone’s specified Chapman route remains a separate position.
comparison: Historical sentence vacatur was 8–1. The seven non-Stone vacating Justices and Thomas retain their historical positions. Stone replaces the historical whole-opinion Chief join with a partial join and a distinct mandatory-remand proposal. Part B consequently has seven rather than eight joins; the Court itself still reserves harmlessness. Authorship is a simulation assignment, not a claim that White historically authored this case.
basis: the remand discussion has a changed controlling coalition and Stone publishes a distinct remedy position; component-specific authority must be shown.

name: General Motors Corp. v. Romein
question: Whether Michigan’s retroactive requirement to repay workers’ compensation offsets violates the Contract Clause or the Due Process Clause.
facts: Michigan’s 1981 legislation permitted coordination of workers’ compensation with specified pension and other benefits, effective March 31, 1982. General Motors and Ford applied offsets to workers injured before that date, and Chambers later accepted that reading. In 1987 Michigan required repayment of those pre-effective-injury offsets, restoring its intended compensation arrangement and equalizing employers that had withheld payments with those that had not. The challenged repayments approached $25 million. The collective agreements predated the coordination law and promised no compensation offset or protection against future statutory adjustment. Michigan’s Supreme Court sustained the repayment requirement; the employers seek reversal on contract and retroactive-due-process grounds.
entering: Article I, §10 prohibits state impairment of contractual obligations; Energy Reserves Group, 459 U.S. 400, and Allied Structural Steel, 438 U.S. 234, require identification of the contract and obligation before impairment analysis. Anderson v. Brand, 303 U.S. 95, requires independent federal examination of the contract question with respectful attention to the state court. United States Trust, 431 U.S. 1, preserves contractual legal force and enforcement, not incorporation of all regulatory law as immutable terms. The Due Process Clause permits retroactive economic regulation with a rational legislative purpose; Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp. v. R.A. Gray & Co., 467 U.S. 717, requires rational justification for retroactivity itself, and Turner Elkhorn, 428 U.S. 1, does not constitutionalize reliance on an old liability schedule. No earlier simulated holding changes either issue.
action: The Michigan Supreme Court’s judgment is affirmed, 9–0, on both constitutional claims.

votes.remedy: No contract reformation, new benefit award, or additional remedy is ordered.

opinions.name: Opinion of the Court
opinions.author: O'Connor
opinions.scope: The absence of a relevant contractual obligation and the rational basis for retroactive repayment; no separate writing.

holdings.title: No relevant contractual obligation was impaired
holdings.rule: A Contract Clause challenge requires an identified contractual obligation that the challenged law impairs; employment regulation does not become an immutable contractual term merely because it governs the relationship. Michigan’s repayment law impairs no offset promise or protected contractual enforcement rule in these employers’ agreements, so substantial-impairment balancing is unnecessary.
holdings.part: O’Connor’s unanimous opinion; all nine Justices adopt the threshold holding.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that the employers have identified no contract right to retain the challenged offsets. Energy Reserves requires a contractual obligation before a court asks how substantially legislation impaired it, and Anderson requires this Court to examine that threshold independently while respecting the state court’s assessment. The agreements predated the coordination law and contained no promise of the later offset. The employers’ alternative argument—that all governing law entered their contracts—would freeze workplace regulation whenever parties contracted. United States Trust protects the legal force and enforceability of actual obligations; it does not convert every statutory payment rule into a promise against legislative revision. Nor has Michigan been shown to have supplied a rule at contracting that constitutionally closed completed payment periods to adjustment. The repayment law leaves the bargained obligations and their enforcement intact. Because the necessary contractual predicate is missing, the Court neither balances a substantial impairment against public necessity nor denies that a genuinely impaired employment contract could receive constitutional protection.
precedents: Energy Reserves Group v. Kansas Power & Light, 459 U.S. 400 — applied: identify the contractual obligation before measuring impairment.
Allied Structural Steel v. Spannaus, 438 U.S. 234 — distinguished: the identified contractual pension obligations there do not create an offset promise here.
Anderson v. Brand, 303 U.S. 95 — applied: federal review independently determines whether the asserted contractual obligation exists.
United States Trust Co. v. New Jersey, 431 U.S. 1 — applied with its boundary: contractual enforceability is protected, but every workplace regulation is not an immutable contract term.
Home Building & Loan Association v. Blaisdell, 290 U.S. 398 — preserved: law may inform actual contractual obligations without freezing all public regulation.
Von Hoffman v. City of Quincy, 4 Wall. 535 — distinguished: withdrawal of contractual enforcement support is absent.
McCracken v. Hayward, 2 How. 608 — distinguished: this law does not remove a remedy enforcing the employers’ contracts.

holdings.title: The retroactive repayment requirement has a rational basis
holdings.rule: Retroactive economic legislation satisfies due process when its retroactive operation rationally advances a legitimate legislative purpose. Requiring repayment of these offsets rationally restores Michigan’s compensation compromise and equalizes affected employers, notwithstanding their reliance on the earlier coordination rule.
holdings.part: O’Connor’s unanimous opinion; the due-process ground independently rejects the second constitutional challenge.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that Michigan could rationally restore the compensation arrangement through repayment of the disputed offsets. R.A. Gray requires a justification for retroactive operation, rather than assuming that a permissible prospective rule automatically validates a retrospective one. That justification exists here: the offsets disrupted the balance struck in the compensation legislation and created different treatment depending on whether an employer had withheld benefits for earlier injuries. Requiring repayment restores that balance and removes the disparity. Turner Elkhorn establishes that economic reliance does not itself prevent a legislature from adjusting burdens connected with prior conduct, and Sperry confirms the legitimacy of allocating comparable financial burdens among affected parties. The employers’ substantial repayment liability therefore does not show irrationality merely because the law unsettles their prior calculations or follows a favorable judicial interpretation. The holding concerns this restoration and equalization measure. It supplies no general immunity for retroactive legislation and no rule that reliance or the scope of a retrospective burden can never matter.
precedents: Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp. v. R.A. Gray & Co., 467 U.S. 717 — applied: retroactivity itself must rationally serve a legitimate purpose.
Usery v. Turner Elkhorn Mining Co., 428 U.S. 1 — applied: reasonable retrospective economic burdens can survive reliance objections.
United States v. Sperry Corp., 493 U.S. 52 — applied: rational allocation of comparable financial burdens is legitimate.

after: Effective March 9, existing contract-threshold and rational-retroactivity doctrine is applied without changing its tests. The employers have no protected offset obligation on these agreements; the repayment law is enforceable. No substantial-impairment balancing rule is added and no categorical validation of retrospective legislation follows.
separate: No separate writing or noted separate position.
procedure: Supreme Court review ends with affirmance. Michigan’s repayment obligation may be enforced on its existing terms; the Court orders no additional award, contract modification, or retained supervision.
stoneCheck: Both approved constitutional grounds, the alternative incorporation-by-law argument, and the limit on substantial-impairment balancing match the unanimous opinion. Existing simulated law supplies no displaced premise. The whole-opinion join is confined to those approved grounds; no new Stone exception or remedy is supplied.
assignment: Stone assigns O’Connor from the unanimous judgment coalition; the opinion retains all nine joins.
audit: White; Blackmun; Stevens; O’Connor; Scalia; Kennedy; Souter; Thomas
Affirm both claims: no offset term under Energy Reserves; rational retrospective restoration under R.A. Gray and Turner Elkhorn.
Retained after comparator; actual agreements and statutory history leave the historical premises intact.
alternatives: The employers’ strongest contract alternative treats settled payment periods and governing law as incorporated obligations; it fails because no applicable promise or enforcement rule is displaced. Their due-process alternative stresses reliance and repayment size; restoring the compensation bargain and equalizing employers rationally justify the retrospective reach. No Justice requires substantial-impairment balancing after the threshold failure.
comparison: The unanimous judgment, grounds, remedy and non-Stone joins match the historical comparator. Stone’s approved incorporation analysis remains within the Court’s actual contract threshold; no additional controlling ground is invented.
basis: 9–0 judgment with no material change from the historical comparator.

name: Williams v. United States
question: When may an appellate court affirm an upward Guidelines departure resting on both permissible and impermissible grounds under 18 U.S.C. §3742(f)?
facts: The district court imposed 27 months, departing from an 18–24 month range on grounds including old convictions and a record of arrests. The circuit recognized that the arrest record was an improper departure basis but affirmed because it regarded the departure as reasonable on other grounds. References to prior same-offense conduct and threats explained selection of the sentence after departure; the Court does not relabel them as independently established departure grounds. Williams seeks correction of the mixed-ground sentence. Whether old nonsimilar convictions can support departure is not clearly presented or briefed, and remains undecided. The convictions are not at issue.
entering: The then-binding Guidelines regime rests on §3553(b); §3742(f)(1) addresses a sentence imposed through incorrect Guidelines application, while §3742(f)(2) separately addresses an unreasonable departure. Section 3553(c) requires the sentencing court’s reasons. Guideline §4A1.3’s policy statement prohibits reliance on an arrest record itself. Rule 52(a) supplies harmless-error treatment for a nonconstitutional error affecting no substantial right. The unresolved statutory issue is the causal and reasonableness relationship, not the later constitutional allocation of sentencing facts. Griffin’s December 3 general-verdict rule concerns a factually unsupported but legally valid object, and supplies no license to rely on an unlawful departure ground. Uncoordinated Dawson and Stringer are not entering law for Williams.
action: The judgment affirming the sentence is vacated and the case remanded to the Seventh Circuit, 7–2.

votes.component: Appellate affirmance of the departure sentence
votes.remedy: The circuit must determine causal harmlessness and separately review departure reasonableness; absent the required findings it must remand for resentencing. The convictions remain intact.

opinions.name: Opinion of the Court
opinions.author: O'Connor
opinions.scope: Invalid-factor error, causal harmlessness with the stated burden sequence, and independent departure-reasonableness review.

opinions.name: Dissent
opinions.author: White
opinions.scope: Would affirm the reasonable departure under a different reading of §3742(f); does not approve the arrest record as a lawful departure factor.

holdings.title: An impermissible departure ground is a Guidelines application error
holdings.rule: A departure based on a factor that the Commission has forbidden, or has already fully considered in the applicable range, rests on an incorrect application of the Guidelines under §3742(f)(1). A policy statement expressly prohibiting a sentencing action is authoritative guidance in applying the relevant Guideline, and an arrest record itself is not a permissible departure ground here.
holdings.part: O’Connor’s opinion, joined by Stone, Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia, Souter and Thomas; seven Justices.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that choosing a departure ground is part of applying the Guidelines. Section 3553(b) limits departure to circumstances not adequately considered by the Commission, and the relevant policy statement expressly excludes an arrest record itself. Treating that prohibition as irrelevant because the sentence departs from the range would remove the very limitation that makes the departure lawful. Section 3742(f)(1) therefore reaches reliance on the invalid factor even if the numerical range was calculated correctly. The competing reading would place every departure solely within reasonableness review under paragraph (2); that approach fails to give effect to the distinct command governing incorrect application. This conclusion does not make every policy statement binding for every purpose. It concerns an express prohibition that guides application of the relevant sentencing provision. Nor does the Court decide whether nonsimilar old convictions may lawfully support a departure: that separate issue was not sufficiently presented for decision in this case.
precedents: No earlier Supreme Court decision is overruled; this is a construction of §§3553(b), 3742(f)(1) and the applicable §4A1.3 prohibition.
Griffin v. United States, simulated December 3, 1991 — kept distinct: unsupported facts under a valid legal theory do not establish the rule for a prohibited sentencing factor.

holdings.title: Harmlessness requires the same sentence without the invalid factor
holdings.rule: Once the challenger establishes reliance on an invalid departure factor, remand is required unless the reviewing court determines from the whole record that the district court would have imposed the same sentence without that factor. The challenger need not additionally prove that the error determined the sentence; the party defending the sentence must persuade the reviewing court that the error was harmless.
holdings.part: O’Connor’s seven-Justice opinion; this is the controlling causal standard under §3742(f)(1) and Rule 52(a).
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that an unlawful factor does not automatically require resentencing, but an appellate court must establish that the error made no difference to the sentence actually chosen. Rule 52(a) permits disregard of an error that affects no substantial right, and §3742(f)(1)’s causal language is consistent with that principle. The challenger first identifies the sentencing court’s reliance on a forbidden factor. Williams has met that burden. Requiring him also to reconstruct the sentencing judge’s unspoken counterfactual would improperly place the consequence of an ambiguous record on the party who established the error. The party defending the sentence must instead persuade the reviewing court, from the whole record, that the judge would have selected the same sentence without it. A conclusion that the judge could lawfully have selected that sentence is insufficient. This statutory error does not acquire Chapman’s constitutional proof standard, and the Court leaves the actual harmlessness determination to the circuit on remand.
precedents: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 52(a) — applied as the governing harmless-error rule for this nonconstitutional sentencing error.
Chapman v. California, 386 U.S. 18 — not imported: the Court adopts no beyond-reasonable-doubt burden for this statutory error.

holdings.title: Departure reasonableness remains a separate condition of affirmance
holdings.rule: Even when an invalid departure ground was harmless under §3742(f)(1), a reviewing court must separately determine under §3742(f)(2) that the departure’s extent is reasonable in light of the valid grounds actually identified by the sentencing court. A reasonable sentence that the district court could have imposed does not establish that the erroneous factor was harmless.
holdings.part: O’Connor’s seven-Justice opinion; both review requirements govern affirmance.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that effect and reasonableness answer different questions. The first asks whether the error influenced the sentence selected; the second asks whether the lawful reasons justify the extent of departure. Section 3742 preserves both inquiries, so satisfaction of one cannot substitute for the other. The circuit found the arrest factor improper but treated the remaining reasons and a reasonable result as sufficient to affirm. That disposition did not resolve whether this judge would have chosen 27 months without the prohibited factor. Nor may an appellate court invent new departure grounds from comments made in choosing a sentence after departure. Solem recognizes the sentencing court’s primary role, and the statutory scheme assigns correction of an improper sentence through remand rather than appellate selection of a new one. The circuit must therefore perform both inquiries on the actual record. The Court decides neither the ultimate reasonable magnitude nor the unpresented question concerning old nonsimilar convictions.
precedents: Solem v. Helm, 463 U.S. 277 — applied for the primary sentencing role of the trial court, not to add a proportionality issue.

after: Effective March 9, §3742(f) now expressly requires separate causal harmlessness and departure-reasonableness review. The changed components are the effect-of-error inquiry, burden sequence after demonstrated reliance, and the relationship between paragraphs (1) and (2). The valid-ground requirement and the district court’s sentencing role remain. No constitutional sentencing-fact rule or blanket policy-statement rule is added.
separate: White, joined by Kennedy, reads the specific departure-review provision as controlling this sentence: once the departure is justified by sufficient lawful reasons and is reasonable, affirmance is permissible. He disputes the majority’s use of §3742(f)(1), not the prohibition on using an arrest record itself. The Court requires causal harmlessness in addition to reasonableness.
procedure: Supreme Court sentence review ends with remand to the Seventh Circuit. That court must decide whether the same sentence would have been imposed and whether the departure is independently reasonable; if either required condition fails, it must remand for resentencing. No new sentence or automatic district-court hearing is imposed now.
stoneCheck: The approved causal rule, challenger’s initial showing, refusal to place the unknowable counterfactual on Williams, separate reasonableness requirement and circuit remand match the Court’s opinion. Stone expressly excludes Chapman’s constitutional quantum and later jury-factfinding rules. No new factual or legal premise changes that position.
assignment: Stone assigns O’Connor from the seven-Justice vacatur coalition; White and Kennedy retain their statutory objection.
audit: Blackmun; Stevens; O’Connor; Scalia; Souter; Thomas
Vacate/remand under §3742(f)(1), Rule 52(a), and a separate §3742(f)(2) inquiry.
Comparator confirms the same statutory grounds and joins; retained.
White; Kennedy
Affirm; specific departure review permits affirmance on adequate lawful reasons and reasonable extent.
Retained after review of White’s dissent; no approval of the arrest ground is inferred.
alternatives: Automatic remand for every invalid factor is too broad because statutory causation and Rule 52(a) allow harmlessness. Reasonableness alone is insufficient under the majority’s reading because it says nothing conclusive about what this judge would have done. White and Kennedy’s statutory alternative survives as a dissent grounded in the departure-specific language, not a different assessment of the arrest record’s validity.
comparison: The 7–2 disposition, O’Connor opinion, White/Kennedy dissent, burden sequence, reserved issue and remedy match the comparator. Stone’s rule coincides with the Court’s at the necessary level of generality.
basis: 7–2 judgment with no material change from the historical comparator.

name: Stringer v. Black
question: Whether Teague bars consideration of the vague-aggravator claim because Maynard or the requested application to Mississippi’s weighing system announced a new rule after Stringer’s sentence became final.
facts: Stringer’s death sentence became final on February 19, 1985. The jury found three aggravating circumstances, including an undefined especially heinous, atrocious or cruel factor, in Mississippi’s system requiring aggravators to be weighed against mitigation. The state appellate court upheld the sentence. The federal district court denied habeas relief both on procedural-default and merits grounds. Following a pre-divergence remand for consideration in light of Clemons, the Fifth Circuit again denied relief on Teague new-rule grounds without deciding the procedural bar. Stringer seeks reversal of that retroactivity ruling. The State invokes finality and the asserted distinction between weighing and nonweighing systems. Whether adequate state correction actually occurred and whether procedural default prevents relief remain for further proceedings.
entering: Teague, 489 U.S. 288, and Butler, 494 U.S. 407, ordinarily prevent federal habeas use of a new procedural rule after finality, subject to exceptions not invoked here. The inquiry first tests whether a later decision announced a new rule, then whether applying an old rule in the requested setting itself would be new. February 19, 1985 fixes the relevant precedent horizon. Godfrey, 446 U.S. 420, rejects unguided heinousness aggravation; Zant, 462 U.S. 862, sustains the distinct nonweighing system while reserving weighing; Barclay, 463 U.S. 939, concerns actual state review and a factor invalid under state law. Maynard, 486 U.S. 356, and Clemons, 494 U.S. 738, are tested for novelty against that prefinality law. Chapman supplies the constitutional harmless-error burden when that corrective route is used. Neither Estelle nor Griffin’s simulated limited rulings displace these doctrines; no March 9 companion supplies pre-1985 law.
action: The Fifth Circuit’s judgment is reversed and the case remanded, 6–3. Teague does not bar this claim on the new-rule ground adopted below.

votes.component: Teague disposition of the vague-aggravator claim
votes.remedy: Further habeas proceedings must address the preserved procedural bar and any constitutionally sufficient state correction. No unconditional writ, automatic life sentence or release is ordered.

opinions.name: Opinion of the Court
opinions.author: Kennedy
opinions.scope: The old-rule determination and the need for genuine reweighing or constitutional harmlessness in the weighing system.

opinions.name: Dissent
opinions.author: Souter
opinions.scope: Would sustain the Teague bar because prefinality precedent did not dictate the Mississippi application.

holdings.title: This application is not a new rule under Teague
holdings.rule: For a sentence final on February 19, 1985, Godfrey already prohibited the unguided heinousness aggravation later addressed in Maynard, and applying that protection to Mississippi’s weighing system does not create a new rule. Teague therefore does not bar consideration of this claim on the ground that Maynard or the corrective principles discussed in Clemons postdated finality.
holdings.part: Kennedy’s opinion, joined by Stone, White, Blackmun, Stevens and O’Connor; six Justices.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that Teague protects reasonable reliance on existing law, not a refusal to recognize what that law already required. Butler requires attention both to the rule announced by a later decision and to whether its proposed application extends the precedent in a new way. Godfrey had already rejected an aggravating phrase that gave the sentencer no meaningful guidance. Maynard applied that same prohibition to closely equivalent language. Mississippi’s formal weighing of aggravation against mitigation makes the defect consequential to sentence selection; it does not exempt the system from the preexisting constitutional protection. Zant expressly distinguished its nonweighing arrangement and supplies no affirmative permission to weigh an invalid factor. The State’s finality argument therefore does not make this particular application novel. Clemons identifies lawful methods of correcting the error rather than first creating the right to challenge it. The Court does not hold that every later capital decision applies retroactively, and it decides no Teague exception or unresolved procedural default.
precedents: Teague v. Lane, 489 U.S. 288 — applied, not replaced: the claim seeks an old rule at the relevant finality date.
Butler v. McKellar, 494 U.S. 407 — applied: both novelty of the later rule and novelty of its application must be considered.
Godfrey v. Georgia, 446 U.S. 420 — applied: meaningful guidance was already required for the heinousness aggravator.
Maynard v. Cartwright, 486 U.S. 356 — treated as applying Godfrey’s old rule to equivalent language.
Clemons v. Mississippi, 494 U.S. 738 — applied as identifying permissible correction, not a newly created protection in this setting.

holdings.title: A weighing error needs a constitutionally adequate cure
holdings.rule: When a capital sentencer weighs a constitutionally invalid aggravating factor against mitigation, remaining valid aggravators do not by themselves cure the error. The state judicial system must supply genuine reweighing without the invalid factor, where authorized, or constitutional harmless-error review establishing that the invalid factor did not affect the sentence; the adequacy of any cure here remains for further proceedings.
holdings.part: Kennedy’s six-Justice opinion; Stone joins the weighing/correction rule with his approved conditional remedy and reserved application.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that an invalid factor placed on the statutory scale cannot be ignored simply by counting the valid factors that remain. Zant sustained a system in which the invalid factor did not do the formal weighing work present here. Barclay also involved actual review of the sentencing choice and a different kind of invalidity; it does not permit automatic affirmance of this constitutional weighing error. Clemons recognizes that a properly authorized state appellate court can itself weigh valid aggravation against mitigation, or can determine under constitutional harmless-error principles that the error did not affect the sentence. Chapman places the harmlessness burden on the State beyond a reasonable doubt. Bare proportionality review or an assertion that other aggravators exist does not establish either correction. The Court leaves the actual state review and the unresolved procedural-default defense to the lower courts. If habeas relief becomes warranted after those matters are resolved, a conditional remedy may permit lawful state correction; death eligibility is not automatically negated.
precedents: Zant v. Stephens, 462 U.S. 862 — distinguished: its nonweighing holding does not automatically cure a weighing-system error.

name: Connecticut National Bank v. Germain
question: Whether 28 U.S.C. §158(d) excludes otherwise available §1292 review of a district court order entered in its bankruptcy appellate capacity.
facts: A bankruptcy trustee sued Connecticut National Bank and demanded a jury trial. The bankruptcy court refused to strike that demand; the district court permitted an appeal, affirmed, and certified an interlocutory question. The bank sought circuit permission under §1292(b). The Second Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, reasoning that §158(d)’s final-order provision implicitly foreclosed interlocutory review. The bank seeks reversal of that jurisdictional dismissal. No jury entitlement or final satisfaction of the discretionary appeal requirements is before this Court for decision.
entering: The 1992 text of §158(a) permits district-court review of final bankruptcy orders and, with leave, interlocutory orders; §158(d) gives courts of appeals jurisdiction over final decisions under the specified bankruptcy provisions. Sections 1291 and 1292 separately govern district-court decisions. Section 1292(b) requires a certified controlling legal question, substantial ground for difference of opinion, material advancement of termination, timely application and circuit permission. Wood v. United States, 16 Pet. 342, permits overlapping statutes to operate absent positive conflict; Ron Pair, 489 U.S. 235, and Rubin, 449 U.S. 424, apply enacted text. MCorp’s December 3 express bank-regulatory preclusion does not imply a bankruptcy appeal restriction. Willy’s collateral Rule 11 holding changes no jurisdictional statute.
action: The jurisdictional dismissal is reversed and the case remanded, 9–0 in judgment.

votes.remedy: The Second Circuit must consider the applicable §1292 route and prerequisites; no automatic interlocutory appeal or jury-trial ruling is granted.

holdings.title: Section 158(d) does not exclude eligible interlocutory review
holdings.rule: Section 158(d) does not preclude court-of-appeals review under §1292 of a district court’s order entered in its bankruptcy appellate capacity. Review remains subject to the particular §1292 route’s requirements, including certification and circuit permission where §1292(b) applies; the provision does not grant an automatic appeal.
holdings.part: Thomas’s opinion, joined by Stone, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter; five Justices adopt the text/coexistence rationale. White, Blackmun, Stevens and O’Connor agree in judgment on their separate stated reasoning.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that an affirmative grant of jurisdiction over final bankruptcy decisions does not silently remove another statute’s grant over specified interlocutory district-court orders. Section 1292 speaks of district courts without distinguishing their original and appellate capacities. Section 158(d) contains no contrary command. Wood requires that both statutes operate where they do not positively conflict, and Ron Pair and Rubin direct attention to the enacted terms. Some overlap with final-order jurisdiction under §1291 does not justify creating an exclusion Congress did not write; the statutes also have different reach, including the bankruptcy appellate panels covered by §158. The bank’s proposed review must therefore be considered under the express interlocutory statute. This does not expand jurisdiction for convenience or dispense with certification, timely application or discretionary acceptance. It also does not extend district-court language to bankruptcy appellate panels without statutory authority. The Court decides the categorical jurisdictional objection only, leaving the jury question and remaining prerequisites for further proceedings.

name: PFZ Properties, Inc. v. Rodriguez
lower: First Circuit, 928 F.2d 28, affirming dismissal reported at 739 F.Supp. 67
question: Whether the operative allegations of delay and irregular land-use administration state a substantive-due-process claim; the grant excludes procedural due process and equal protection, and the takings theory was abandoned.
facts: PFZ relied on preliminary project approvals and asserted an entitlement to development permits after submitting drawings. Its amended complaint alleged prolonged administrative delay and irregular treatment. The district court dismissed, and the First Circuit affirmed. On rehearing the circuit refused to enlarge the complaint through belated reliance on a pretrial order. The official argument exposed disagreement over the source and nature of the property interest, which drawings were properly before the agency, and whether asserted deliberate obstruction was within the operative pleading. Alleged bad faith and a sham process are party characterizations, not adjudicated findings. PFZ sought reversal; respondents defended dismissal. The limited grant does not permit resolution of the separate procedural claim.
entering: Section 1983 enforces independently established federal rights; Roth, 408 U.S. 564, identifies sources of property entitlement, and Ewing, 474 U.S. 214, assumed a property interest while rejecting the particular substantive claim. Daniels, 474 U.S. 327, distinguishes tortious administration from a constitutional deprivation. The simulated Collins decision of February 26 rejects an extra freestanding §1983 abuse element, denies a general voluntary-workplace safety guarantee, and rejects its particular alleged safety omissions as constitutional arbitrariness; it adopts no general land-use rule. Available state review does not itself answer whether an independently substantive wrong occurred. The granted substantive question, the operative complaint, and the rejected rehearing enlargement constrain merits review. The Court may dismiss an unsuitable writ without creating a merits rule.
action: The writ of certiorari is dismissed as improvidently granted. Chief Justice Stone dissents.

votes.remedy: The First Circuit’s judgment remains in place without Supreme Court endorsement of its reasoning. Stone would reach and affirm dismissal of the substantive claim on his stated narrow ground.

name: United States v. R. L. C.
question: Whether the juvenile-detention ceiling in 18 U.S.C. §5037(c)(1)(B) incorporates the maximum Guidelines sentence authorized for the comparable adult offender and offense.
facts: At age 16, R.L.C. caused a child’s death while driving recklessly and intoxicated in Indian country. After a bench adjudication the district court found juvenile delinquency corresponding to involuntary manslaughter and imposed three years, the offense statute’s adult maximum. The Eighth Circuit held that §5037’s adult comparison incorporates the Guidelines; the agreed comparable adult range was 15–21 months. It vacated and remanded. Without a Government stay, the district court subsequently imposed 18 months, which R.L.C. has served. The Government seeks restoration of the original statutory-maximum approach, so possible renewed detention prevents mootness. No specific additional departure basis is established by this record for present decision.
entering: Section 5037(c)(1)(B) limits qualifying juvenile detention to the maximum imprisonment authorized if this juvenile were tried and convicted as an adult; the separate age limit remains. Section 3553(b) makes the adult Guidelines range binding absent an authorized departure. Sections 1112 and 1153 supply the offense and jurisdictional predicates. Villamonte-Marquez, 462 U.S. 579, supports continued controversy where adverse relief may be restored despite completion of the reduced sentence. Bass, 404 U.S. 336, Bifulco, 447 U.S. 381, Moskal, 498 U.S. 103, Hughey, 495 U.S. 411, and Chapman v. United States, 500 U.S. 453, supply distinct date-eligible lenity formulations; no current majority methodological revision is assumed. The March 9 Williams record is now committed and effective: invalid departure grounds require causal harmlessness review and a separate reasonable extent, and an express prohibition in the applicable policy statement cannot be ignored. That refresh supplies no new departure fact here and changes no provisional result. The other March 24 decisions are not entering law.
action: The Eighth Circuit’s judgment is affirmed, 7–2. The adult Guidelines ceiling governs the statutory comparison.

holdings.title: The juvenile ceiling incorporates the lawful adult Guidelines maximum
holdings.rule: For juvenile detention governed by §5037(c)(1)(B), the maximum authorized adult sentence includes the applicable Guidelines ceiling for the comparable offender and offense, subject to a properly supported lawful departure. The Guidelines determine that upper limit only; they do not impose a Guidelines minimum or otherwise require plenary adult Guidelines sentencing for the juvenile.
holdings.part: Parts I, II-A and III of Souter’s opinion, joined by Stone, White, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas; seven Justices. The legislative-history and competing lenity explanations do not command five votes.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that a sentence is authorized only if it complies with statutes that limit the sentencing judge as well as those that define the offense. Section 3553(b)’s command to apply the Guidelines is itself statutory. The Government’s focus on the three-year offense maximum therefore does not establish that an adult court could impose that term despite the applicable Guidelines ceiling. Section 5037 compares this juvenile with an adult sentenced in comparable circumstances, which requires identifying the proper adult range. Here that range is 15–21 months, absent a supported lawful departure. This conclusion does not make the adult Guidelines govern juvenile disposition in full. The juvenile court retains its discretion below the applicable cap and remains subject to the other statutory limitations. The dissent’s concern for rehabilitation does not remove the enacted upper limit, while calculating the limit does not require adoption of every adult sentencing rule. No particular additional departure ground is approved and no common methodological rule for lenity is announced.
precedents: United States v. Villamonte-Marquez, 462 U.S. 579 — applied to the threshold controversy: possible restoration of the longer detention keeps the case live.
Williams v. United States, simulated March 9, 1992 — preserved in the entering-law relationship: only lawful departure grounds can support a higher adult ceiling; this case approves none.
Moskal v. United States, 498 U.S. 103 — not overruled or revised by a majority; the competing lenity explanations remain noncontrolling.
United States v. Bass, 404 U.S. 336, and Bifulco v. United States, 447 U.S. 381 — remain date-eligible lenity authorities; no common new timing rule is adopted here.

A lawful departure can affect that ceiling, but none is established here; the adult Guidelines minimum does not become a juvenile floor. Seven join the Court’s text/result sections; Souter’s history/lenity sections have three votes. Scalia’s legislative-history restriction and Thomas’s qualification remain noncontrolling; Marks is unnecessary for the seven-Justice ceiling and supplies no synthetic majority methodology.

Scalia, joined by Kennedy and Thomas, would not use legislative history to resolve textual punishment ambiguity against the accused. Thomas separately stresses that established legal rules of construction precede lenity. Stone relies on text and statutory context, uses residual lenity only to confirm narrower punishment, and preserves juvenile discretion below the ceiling. O’Connor, joined by Blackmun, dissents: in her view, the offense-statute maximum preserves the separate rehabilitative scheme, and calculating an adult range imports procedures Congress did not require. The Court adopts the cap without resolving those methodological disagreements.

name: Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co. v. Darden
question: Whether ERISA’s definition of employee incorporates general common-law agency principles or the circuit’s benefits-expectation, reliance and bargaining-power test.
facts: Darden sold Nationwide insurance under agreements providing retirement benefits and forfeiture conditions tied to post-termination competition. After termination he sold competitors’ policies, and Nationwide denied benefits. The district court initially regarded him as an independent contractor. The Fourth Circuit instead required reasonable benefit expectations, reliance and insufficient bargaining power; on remand Darden prevailed under that test and the circuit affirmed. Nationwide seeks application of the common-law employee category. The United States supports reversal but proposed some remedial modification of the common-law approach. The circuit did not finally decide Darden’s status under the proper agency test. The denied cross-petition concerning the Extended Earnings Plan is outside review.
entering: ERISA §§1002(6), 1002(7), 1053(a) and 1132(a) distinguish employee status, participant eligibility, vesting and enforcement. The employee definition is circular. Reid, 490 U.S. 730, presumes that an undefined employee term incorporates general common-law agency meaning absent contrary statutory direction. United Insurance, 390 U.S. 254, requires assessment of all relationship incidents without one decisive factor. Hearst, 322 U.S. 111, and Silk, 331 U.S. 704, involved different statutes and subsequent congressional responses; Rutherford Food, 331 U.S. 722, concerns the FLSA’s broader suffer-or-permit definition. Lechmere’s January 27 NLRA access holding supplies no ERISA status test. No March 9 holding displaces Reid or changes this classification question; other March 24 opinions are not entering law.
action: The Fourth Circuit’s judgment is reversed and the case remanded, 9–0, for application of general common-law agency principles.

votes.remedy: The lower court must determine Darden’s status under all relevant agency factors; no final employee classification or benefits award is made here.

opinions.name: Opinion of the Court
opinions.author: Souter
opinions.scope: The general common-law agency test, its complete multifactor character, rejection of the expectations test and remand; no separate writing.

holdings.title: ERISA employee status follows general common-law agency
holdings.rule: ERISA’s circular definition of employee incorporates the general common law of agency, not a particular State’s law or a substitute test of benefit expectations, reliance and bargaining power. Courts must weigh all incidents of the relationship—including control over manner and means, skill, tools, work location, duration, assignment rights, scheduling discretion, payment, assistants, regular-business integration, the hiring party’s business, benefits and tax treatment—with no single factor decisive.
holdings.part: Souter’s unanimous opinion; all nine Justices adopt the statutory definition and multifactor application requirement.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that an expectation of retirement benefits cannot itself establish membership in the employee category Congress protected. Reid presumes that a statutory employee term carries its settled agency meaning unless Congress directs otherwise. ERISA’s circular definition supplies no such direction, and its general protective purpose does not identify a different class. United Insurance requires weighing all incidents of the relationship; a contractual label or one favorable factor does not settle the matter. Hearst and Silk do not justify replacing this inquiry with remedial purpose, particularly after Congress’s contrary responses to their interpretations. Rutherford Food remains different because the FLSA expressly reaches work suffered or permitted, language ERISA lacks. The circuit’s expectations test also assumes the disputed statutory entitlement when it disregards the agreed forfeiture condition, and its reliance prong can treat identical jobs differently according to personal savings choices. The proper inquiry concerns the employment relationship. Darden’s ultimate classification and any resulting vesting or forfeiture consequence remain for remand.
precedents: Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730 — applied to ERISA: general common-law agency is the default meaning of an unhelpfully defined employee term.
NLRB v. United Insurance Co., 390 U.S. 254 — applied: all incidents must be assessed with no single decisive factor.
NLRB v. Hearst Publications, 322 U.S. 111 — limited as a general interpretive model: purpose alone does not displace agency meaning in ERISA.
United States v. Silk, 331 U.S. 704 — its general purposive emphasis is not followed for undefined employee terms; Reid supplies the governing presumption.
Rutherford Food Corp. v. McComb, 331 U.S. 722 — distinguished and preserved: FLSA’s broader express definition supports its different reach.
Kelley v. Southern Pacific, 419 U.S. 318; Baker v. Texas & Pacific, 359 U.S. 227; Robinson v. Baltimore & Ohio, 237 U.S. 84 — retained as supporting applications of ordinary agency meaning.

after: Effective March 24, Reid’s presumption governs ERISA’s employee definition, with the complete multifactor agency inquiry and no decisive single factor. The circuit’s expectations/reliance/bargaining-power substitute is rejected. FLSA’s broader statutory category remains distinct; Darden’s status, available benefits and independent state-contract remedies are not decided.
separate: No separate writing or noted separate position.
procedure: Supreme Court review ends with remand to the Fourth Circuit for the proper classification inquiry and further proceedings consistent with that result. Neither Darden’s employee status nor an entitlement to benefits is finally determined. The excluded cross-petition issue is not reopened.

Benefits may be a factor but do not replace classification; no corporation-specific or employee-specific exception is added. The denied cross-petition and actual prior remands do not change the approved scope.
assignment: Stone assigns Souter from the unanimous reversal coalition; all nine join the opinion.
audit: White; Blackmun; Stevens; O’Connor; Scalia; Kennedy; Souter; Thomas
Reverse/remand; Reid and United Insurance govern ERISA’s circular definition.
Retained after comparator; no intervening simulated law changes the statutory premise, and no special remedial variation is adopted.
alternatives: The circuit’s benefit-expectation approach invokes ERISA’s protective purpose but assumes coverage in defining the covered class and makes status depend on personal reliance. A modified common-law approach likewise lacks a textual basis for changing the agency rule. The common-law route respects Reid while leaving factual weighing and ultimate coverage to remand.
comparison: The unanimous disposition, Souter opinion, factor-based rule, precedent distinctions and remedy match the comparator after Stone’s compatible substitution.
basis: 9–0 judgment with no material change from the historical comparator.

name: United States v. Wilson
question: Whether the sentencing court or the Attorney General through the Bureau of Prisons initially computes presentence detention credit under §3585(b), and at what stage.
facts: Tennessee detained Wilson beginning October 5, 1988. The federal district court imposed a 96-month Hobbs Act sentence on November 29, 1989 and refused the requested state-custody credit. On December 12 the state court imposed its sentence, credited 429 days, and transferred Wilson to federal custody, when his federal sentence began. The Sixth Circuit held that the federal sentencing court should have awarded credit. The Government seeks reversal; Wilson relies on Congress’s deletion of the Attorney General’s name from former §3568 and the federal sentence’s earlier date. The Court reviews actor and timing, not a separate challenge to a completed BOP calculation.
entering: Section 3585(b) mandates qualifying official-detention credit before sentence commencement only for time not credited against another sentence. Section 3621(a) assigns federal sentence administration to BOP. Former §3568 named the Attorney General; the complete revision uses the passive voice and changes other conditions. Otte, 419 U.S. 43, and Gwaltney, 484 U.S. 49, treat verb tense as significant; Russello, 464 U.S. 16, supplies a rebuttable inference from changed statutory wording; Robertson, 268 U.S. 619, cautions against assuming departure from established practice. Administrative review under the contemporaneous regulations and subsequent judicial review remain available. McCarthy’s March 4 damages-only Bivens holding addresses a process unable to provide money compensation; a credit computation process can supply this requested relief, so that result is not transplanted. The actual simulated Wolas concerns §547(c)(2)’s ordinary-course debt rule; it does not decide who computes detention credit. March 9 decisions do not displace these statutory premises.
action: The Sixth Circuit’s judgment is reversed, 7–2. The Attorney General through BOP makes the initial credit computation after the federal sentence begins.

holdings.title: BOP makes the initial credit computation after commencement
holdings.rule: Section 3585(b) does not authorize a district court to compute detention credit at sentencing; the Attorney General through BOP must make the initial computation after the federal sentence commences. Administrative review and proper subsequent judicial review remain available, so the calculation is not unreviewable discretion.
holdings.part: Thomas’s opinion, joined by Stone, Blackmun, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter; seven Justices.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that the credit calculation belongs to administration of the sentence after it begins. Section 3585(b) looks to detention already spent before commencement and to credit already given against another sentence. Otte and Gwaltney show why the verbs’ temporal meaning matters: at sentencing, the court may not know when detention will end or when another sentence will receive credit. Section 3621 assigns administration of the federal term to BOP, which must determine the remaining time and therefore must compute the statutory credit. Congress’s deletion of the Attorney General’s name during a complete rewrite does not affirmatively transfer this task to sentencing judges. Russello’s inference from changed wording is overcome by the present text and structure; Robertson cautions against assuming an unexplained abandonment of established administration. The contrary approach would make the initial decision depend on incomplete information. Prisoners retain administrative review and proper judicial review; neither a new credit award nor an unreviewable executive power follows.
precedents: Otte v. United States, 419 U.S. 43 — applied: Congress’s choice of verb tense informs statutory timing.
Gwaltney of Smithfield v. Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 — applied for the same temporal-text principle.
Russello v. United States, 464 U.S. 16 — applied as a rebuttable inference, overcome here by the rewritten text and administration scheme.
Robertson v. Railroad Labor Board, 268 U.S. 619 — applied: a departure from long-established procedure is not lightly inferred.
McCarthy v. Madigan, simulated March 4, 1992 — distinguished: its damages-only process could not provide the requested relief, unlike a credit computation process.

holdings.title: Credit already applied to another sentence cannot be counted again
holdings.rule: Section 3585(b) forbids federal detention credit for time already credited against another sentence when the federal sentence begins. A defendant cannot avoid that condition merely because the federal sentencing hearing occurred before the other court awarded its credit.
holdings.part: Thomas’s seven-Justice opinion; the no-double-credit condition supports the actor/timing disposition.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that the sequence of sentencing hearings does not create a right to count the same detention twice. Section 3585(b) expressly excludes time credited against another sentence, and its commencement-based calculation gives that condition practical effect. Wilson’s federal hearing occurred before Tennessee awarded its 429 days, but the award preceded his transfer and the start of the federal term. Measuring eligibility only at the earlier hearing would make the federal credit depend on the happenstance of which court sentenced first. Turkette’s instruction to avoid absurd statutory results supports rejecting that arbitrary consequence. The revised provision also broadens some eligible detention and changes other language, so preserving administrative calculation does not render the revision meaningless. This Court does not calculate a fresh numerical credit, define every form of official detention, or decide a later challenge to BOP’s application. It holds only that the established state credit cannot be disregarded on the timing theory accepted below.
precedents: United States v. Turkette, 452 U.S. 576 — applied: avoid an arbitrary statutory result unsupported by the text’s purpose.

after: Effective March 24, §3585(b)’s initial actor and timing are settled: BOP computes after commencement, applying the prohibition on credit already used against another sentence. The changed wording does not transfer initial calculation to the sentencing judge. Proper review remains, and McCarthy creates no exemption for this relief-capable administrative process. No particular BOP calculation or universal definition of official detention is adjudicated.
separate: Stevens, joined by White, would permit the sentencing court to resolve a ripe credit entitlement when counsel and the record are available, leaving ministerial arithmetic or later adjustments to the appropriate official. He reads the passive wording and placement in the sentencing chapter as allowing shared responsibility and rejects the premise that occasional incomplete information bars every sentencing-stage determination. The Court instead adopts initial administrative computation after commencement. The dissent does not claim unreviewable executive discretion or discard the statutory no-double-credit language.
procedure: Supreme Court review ends in reversal of the circuit’s direction to award credit at sentencing. BOP remains responsible for the initial calculation after commencement, with administrative and judicial review through proper channels. The Court awards no days of credit and makes no new detention order.
stoneCheck: The approved actor, timing, anti-double-credit rule, and proper review channels match Thomas’s opinion. McCarthy is revalidated as a claim-and-remedy-specific holding, not a general bar to credit exhaustion. The actual state credit and custody sequence are consistent with Stone’s approved premise. No choice concerning what qualifies as official detention is supplied.
assignment: Stone assigns Thomas from the seven-Justice reversing coalition; Stevens and White retain their dissent.

alternatives: The Court’s administration reading unifies completed detention, other-sentence credit and §3621 responsibility. Stevens’s alternative permits a court to decide ripe legal entitlements without doing every later calculation and emphasizes counsel and prompt certainty. The majority finds the specified commencement point incompatible with initial sentencing credit; the dissent regards that prohibition as unnecessarily rigid. Neither view permits inventing the actual BOP award.
